posts.title: Structuring CSS So It Does Not Fall Apart
posts.titlePs: CSS داسې تنظیم کړه چې نه خرابیږي
posts.excerpt: How a token layer, a reset, core styles and a responsive layer keep a stylesheet readable long after the first week.
posts.excerptPs: څنګه د ټوکنونو، ریسټ، اصلي سټایلونو او ریسپانسیو طبقو پر بنسټ CSS د اوږدې مودې لپاره د لوستلو وړ پاتې کېږي.
posts.content:
Why most stylesheets rot

Most CSS problems are not caused by CSS. They are caused by a lack of structure. Colors get hardcoded in twelve places, spacing values become arbitrary, and every new component reinvents a card.

Four layers

A simple four-layer split solves most of it:

  • variables.css — every color, radius, shadow and spacing value in one place
  • reset.css — a predictable baseline across browsers
  • style.css — components and layout built only from tokens
  • responsive.css — media queries, kept in one file

The rule that matters

Never write a raw color or a raw pixel value inside a component. If a value is not in the token layer, add it there first. This single rule is what keeps a project consistent six months later.

What you get

Theme switching becomes a variable swap. A rebrand becomes one file. And a new component is assembled from existing tokens instead of invented from scratch.

posts.title: Accessible Forms: Small Details That Change Everything
posts.titlePs: د لاسرسي وړ فورمې: کوچني توضیحات چې ټول بدلوي
posts.excerpt: Labels, error messages, focus states and validation timing — the four things that decide whether a form is usable.
posts.excerptPs: لیبلونه، د تېروتنې پیغامونه، د فوکس حالت او د اعتبار وخت — څلور هغه څه چې د فورمې کارونې وړتیا ټاکي.
posts.content:
Start with a real label

A placeholder is not a label. Placeholders disappear the moment someone starts typing, and screen readers handle them inconsistently. Always use a real <label> tied to the input with for and id.

Validate at the right moment

Validating while someone is still typing is hostile. Validate on blur and on submit. Show the error next to the field, not in a banner at the top of the page.

Say what went wrong

"Invalid input" tells the user nothing. "Please enter a valid email address, for example name@example.com" tells them exactly what to do.

Never remove focus

Keyboard users need to see where they are. Use :focus-visible with a clear, high-contrast outline. Removing outlines without a replacement is one of the most common accessibility failures on the web.

Announce success too

Use role="status" on the success message so screen reader users are told the form submitted. Without it, nothing appears to happen.

posts.title: Building an Interface That Works in Both LTR and RTL
posts.titlePs: داسې انټرفیس جوړول چې LTR او RTL دواړو کې کار کوي
posts.excerpt: Logical CSS properties, direction-aware icons and the real cost of treating RTL as an afterthought.
posts.excerptPs: منطقي CSS خصوصیات، د لوري پوه ایکونونه او هغه لګښت چې RTL د وروستي فکر په توګه لري.
posts.content:
Stop using left and right

Physical properties like margin-left and padding-right break the moment direction flips. Use logical properties instead: margin-inline-start, padding-inline-end, inset-inline-start.

Let the document carry direction

Set dir="rtl" on the <html> element. Everything else — text alignment, flex order, scrollbars — follows automatically. Fighting it with manual overrides creates more bugs than it fixes.

Icons need direction awareness

Arrows, chevrons and back buttons must flip. Logos, play buttons and clocks must not. Treat this as a per-icon decision, not a global one.

Typography is different

Arabic-script fonts need different line heights and letter spacing than Latin fonts. Set a separate font stack for RTL and adjust line-height — the Latin values will look cramped.

Test with real content

Short English strings hide layout problems. Test with real Pashto sentences, which are often longer and have different word shapes. That is where the bugs actually appear.
